lesson.title: Zooming In Forever: The Instantaneous Rate of Change
lesson.summary: Shrinking the interval used for average rate of change down toward a single point, using a limit, produces the instantaneous rate of change: exactly how fast a function is changing at one precise moment rather than across a stretch.
lesson.body:
The average rate of change answers how fast f changes across an interval, but it cannot say how fast f is changing at one exact instant, since a single point has no width to divide by. Instantaneous rate solves this by taking the average rate of change over an interval starting at a point a and letting the width of that interval shrink toward zero, using a limit. Writing the interval as [a, a+h], the average rate of change is [f(a+h) - f(a)] divided by h, and the instantaneous rate of change at x=a is defined as the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(a+h) - f(a)] divided by h. This limiting value, when it exists, is exactly what is later called the derivative of f at a.

Let f(x) = x^2 and find the instantaneous rate of change at x=2. Set up the average rate of change over [2, 2+h]: [f(2+h) - f(2)] divided by h = [(2+h)^2 - 4] divided by h. Expand the square: (2+h)^2 = 4 + 4h + h^2, so the numerator becomes 4 + 4h + h^2 - 4 = 4h + h^2. Dividing by h, valid since h is approaching but not equal to 0, gives 4 + h. Now take the limit as h approaches 0: the limit of (4 + h) is 4. So the instantaneous rate of change of f(x) = x^2 at x=2 is exactly 4.

This symbolic answer can be checked by computing average rates of change over intervals that shrink toward x=2. Over [2, 2.1]: f(2) = 4, f(2.1) = 4.41, average rate = (4.41 - 4)/0.1 = 0.41/0.1 = 4.1. Over [2, 2.01]: f(2.01) = 4.0401, average rate = (4.0401 - 4)/0.01 = 0.0401/0.01 = 4.01. Over [2, 2.001]: f(2.001) = 4.004001, average rate = 0.004001/0.001 = 4.001. As the interval width shrinks from 0.1 to 0.01 to 0.001, the average rate of change moves from 4.1 to 4.01 to 4.001, closing in on 4 exactly as the symbolic limit predicted.

This machinery gives back a familiar answer when applied to a linear function, which is a useful sanity check. For f(x) = 3x + 5, the average rate of change over [x, x+h] is [f(x+h) - f(x)] divided by h = [3(x+h) + 5 - (3x + 5)] divided by h = [3x + 3h + 5 - 3x - 5] divided by h = 3h/h = 3, for every h that is not 0. Taking the limit as h approaches 0 leaves 3 unchanged, since there is no h left in the expression at all. The instantaneous rate of change of a linear function is therefore the same constant 3 at every single point x, exactly matching the constant slope described back in the introduction to rate of change, confirming that the general instantaneous-rate definition correctly reduces to ordinary slope whenever the function is a straight line.

This construction depends on everything covered so far: it starts from average rate of change, uses the algebraic setup of the difference quotient, and requires the formal machinery of a limit to make sense of dividing by an interval width that is heading to zero without ever actually reaching it. The reason this limit is worth taking at all, rather than just picking a very small h and calling it close enough, is that the limit gives an exact value, 4 in this example, rather than an approximation that depends on an arbitrary choice of how small is small enough.

Instantaneous rate of change is what distinguishes an average speed reading over a whole trip from a speedometer reading at one exact moment behind the wheel: the speedometer is reporting an instantaneous rate, not an average one. This is the quantity that the secant line construction, examined next, approximates more and more closely as its two points are pulled together.
